item.title: Another product of The Factory: Another product of The Factory
item.content:encoded:
It's a set of six simple table settings in boxes. If you take a piece (like a fork or a plate) out of the box and set it on a table, it locks onto that position. If you move it somewhere else and leave it alone for an hour, it will go back to where it belongs. If you sufficiently destroy the table, the pieces will return to their original boxes.

This is a very simple, old-school, "normal thing with a gimmick" kind of idea. Has it been done before? How can I make an article about this more fun and interesting? Is this just a bad or boring idea? All feedback and questions are appreciated! :-)

item.title: Green light my idea: Forum Crit Team - Staff Post
item.content:encoded:
You're really going to have to expand on this a lot more before anyone can give you any useful critique on this idea. Remember: you get 400 words in the final four sections to explain this, and you've currently used 24 words.

This doesn't even consider that parts of this feel inconsistent: 'The skip causes instantaneous los of cohesion in most solid material' and "It causes crystalizing of bone if you touch it" are not two things that feel intuitively like they connect and it needs more detail to help us understand your idea. Your post summary mentions D-9876 but there's no mention of who they are or what they have to do with this SCP.

I would highly recommend editing the original post to cover more detail about what the SCP is and what the article is about, using the 'Edit' button under the blue 'Options' button at the bottom right corner of the post.

item.title: An in-universe parody of Are We Cool Yet.: Re: An in-universe parody of Are We Cool Yet.
item.content:encoded:
I should make it clear that the article itself isn't meant to be a parody, in-universe it's just a regular foundation document like any other. The statue itself is a disillusioned AWCY creating something to mock AWCY. Essentially saying they're all just psychopaths making harmful objects and justifying it with a bunch of bullshit about creating 'art'. I don't picture the artist responsible as trying to be funny really, but mocking the organisation he is/was apart of.

Now that I think about it, it's sort of the reverse of -1802, the AWCY robot that makes fun of the foundation.

And I do realise now that the concept does make the foundation look pretty incompetent. I think the statue killing one or two people before the foundation ramps up its precautions would fit a lot better, and for there to be a solid reason why the foundation tries to find out what the piece is saying. I'm currently mulling over what exactly convinces the foundation to try and 'interpret' the work rather than lock it away completely, and I'm thinking maybe it's just the one senior researcher who has a background in anomalous art and becomes obsessed with the piece, perhaps his personal notes are the things being partially logged in the article.

As to your second-last paragraph @cybersqyd - that sounds like a really interesting SCP idea for a much better writer than me, I don't think my ability extends to deep-dive analysis of art history.

item.title: TICKY TAFFY TOWN (Seeking Greenlight): Re: TICKY TAFFY TOWN (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
This feels pretty reminiscent of something like SCP-993 or SCP-2030 without really doing anything hugely new with the concept. It also feels like it relies really heavily on shock horror, particularly that of massive child death, and I would really urge you to not do that.

Beyond this: your actual pitch is too heavily summarised, which makes it really hard to tell how all the stuff fits together. E.g., you mention the 'children's show and candy are mysteriously causing disappearances' but there's not really any indication of how this works: is it like, people on the show disappear? People who watch it? How does the candy tie in?

There's talk of an exploration log in the middle of the central narrative which seems fine; but you mention that 'Addendums and follow up memos follow to round out the story' but I don't really have a feel for either a) what the core of the story is or b) how they round out the story; and I'm left feeling…not very enthused by any part of this.

item.title: Seeking Greenlight - Mirror Mirror: Re: Seeking Greenlight - Mirror Mirror
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

People in close proximity to the mirror are mimetically compelled to want to stare into the mirror.

I would advise not doing this: forcing the mirror to be used like this kinda removes your ability to explore why someone might choose to look into the mirror; but it also removes some of the danger in that, you can't as easily have 'I caught a glimpse of the mirror in a reflect' happen say because guess what, the mirror forces you to start into it.

Any sentient non-anomalous entity that stares into the mirror will undergo transfiguration based on some internal quality, desire or fear.

So like, what are these transfigurations like? Are we talking minor stuff like 'their hair colour changes' or are we talking major stuff like 'they turn into a rabbit' or what?

Most transfiguration seem to be malicious in nature, however some notable exceptions have been observed.

What do you mean by 'malicious'? Like as in 'the transfiguration is done to hurt the person being transformed' or as in 'the transfiguration turns them into a monster'?

May be vaguely linked to SCP-352

I wouldn't cross-link to an old series 1 SCP like this but *shrugs*.

Expands the lore of SCP's with a strong connection to specific countries (Russia)

How does it do this? It feels like this is just by piggybacking off 352 but?

Transfiguration based SCP's aren't terribly common on the wiki. Especially ones that aren't inherently detrimental.

Earlier you said that most transfigurations 'seem to be malicious in nature' so this does feel like something that's inherently detrimental?

The Nature of the SCP also compels people to try and utilize it for good

How does this happen? It feels like it just compels people to look into it? But there's also not really any indication of how they could use it for good at all?

I have little experience using HTML formatting and templates.

The How To Write an SCP guide and SCP Style Resource include a bunch of examples of basic and advanced formatting. You can also hit "+ Options" at the bottom of an article and then "Page Source" to see how an article creates various formatting things.

I have spent a lot of time so far talking about relatively minor aspects of this but I want to talk about my core concern with this: this is too much of a description of a weird magical item at the moment; it feels a lot like this is the kinda thing that I'd expect to see as a cursed item (or a trap) in a game of DnD and not like the kinda thing I'd expect to see as a SCP. The core of writing a good SCP is that what you do with a SCP is a lot more important than what a SCP can do: if you just describe the SCP, you will likely have a lot of difficulty in getting a reader to care about what happens, and even modern short SCPs that don't have long addendums work because at their core, they have an interesting thing with shocking implications. This doesn't have that, but it also doesn't really have an exploration of what the SCP does, and without giving this more narrative weight, I don't see it working.

There's a bunch of guides in the Comprehensive Guide Hub, particularly in the 'Misc. Essays' section at the end, that talk more about how you can tell interesting stories within the SCP format; but often the best way to learn is to read a lot of modern SCPs.

item.title: A Simple Bar: Re: A Simple Bar
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

I'm not fully convinced by this as a SCP article: like, the actual emotional beats here and the story you're telling are pretty fun but it feels like having to tell this largely from the Foundation's perspective will feel weird and like, blunten the emotional impact.

Indeed, the Foundation's involvement here feels really awkward as a whole: if they know this place is anomalous, it really feels like they'd do more to keep it in containment than they do, and also that they wouldn't like…just let people go there as patrons? It also feels like a Foundation site is a strange place for a bar, like, I guess they function as small towns but it feels odd that the person thinks this is going to be the most effective place to put the bar and it feels odder that they turn out to be right?

I guess, when it comes down to it, what I am saying is that I think this would be best as a tale from the perspective of the bartender where the Foundation are at best minor side characters, or possibly a secondary antagonist. Like, if the story was the Foundation trying to shut down the bar, and the bartender trying to do everything in his power and being forced to keep moving the bar, then it feels like you'd have a lot more effective of a story; and it also feels like it'd help explain why e.g. the bartender isn't managing to make enough money. (I would still tell this as a tale from the perspective of the bartender if you want to do that though btw).

item.title: The Screen Crawler: Re: The Screen Crawler
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

So this is like…clearly a narrative focussed around the recovery log and the exploration log; but I only really have a broad strokes view of what happens in both, and neither seems…hugely interesting to me to read? My concern is that it sounds like both are just going to end up being very matter of fact things that don't really add much narratively to this; and I'd really like to know a little more about your plans around them before I'd be willing to even consider greenlighting this.

My, other concern is that the SCP feels…a little too x-man-y and complex to me: it has a range of anomalous powers that are kinda thematically linked but it feels a bit lacking in cohesion: elements like the pocket dimension, and the 'extend all organs and bones' part feel sort of tacked on in an effort to make this more interesting and my concern is that you've kinda mistaken 'can do lots of cool things' for 'interesting idea to read about'.

I guess really what I want to know is how you're really wanting to convey a sense of horror to a reader here: the very short summary of both the recovery mission and the exploration log makes it feel like they were both kinda carried out with minimal effort and danger, and that feels very unconducive to a good horror atmosphere, y'know?

I'm also not convinced that a lengthy section on how the Foundation got this into containment will feel that satisfying to read: it kinda feels like the sort of thing were the ConProcs would give away that it's in Containment, and so the rest of the article is just…moving pieces into the position we already know it's in? It feels to me that focussing on what happens once it's contained might be more interesting; though it feels like this is the kinda SCP that might force that into a generic containment breach story and I would strongly urge you to try and find a different angle to that.

item.title: Data not redacted? (Seeking Greenlight): Re: Data not redacted? (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

See…my core concern here is that there's not really a sense of consequences/stakes here: like, it's fine to have the ethics committee be secretly be behind this but there's not really a like…clear feeling of there being a motivation for it, and it doesn't really feel like it leads them to achieve anything or to the reader's understanding of this being significantly changed.

Like, it being a power play to allow the EC to gain an upper hand over the O5 council is fine but there's not really a clear idea of:

  1. why the EC wants to do this
  2. whether the EC are actually successful
  3. what the EC are going to do if it is successful

My feelings are that if this is to work, you'll likely want to actually make the EC/O5 interplay part of the text because it's the interesting part of this but it's also the part which actually feels like it has stakes; and in turn, you'll need to really consider what the framing is that allows you to do this: it's very possible to have the reader be canonically on one or the other as they read this; and in turn, to have partial information about what the other wants.

I don't think the current framing works because it relies too much on the mystery of this being interesting inherently without you doing anything to show why the mystery matters. This said: it's very possible that this is just my opinion and other reviewers will disagree.

item.title: @fterlife.net (seeking greenlights): Re: @fterlife.net (seeking greenlights)
item.content:encoded:
Hello anhphamvn! let's take a look :) -sorry about the late response time!

SAND

+ show block
– hide block


The concept:

Elevator Pitch: An online database. When an X digits number is inputted, it might allows the user to enter a page with documents about a deceased person and an AI resembling that person. At the moment, the foundation has only gained access to a small amount of pages. Others are locked and require "Administrator's permission".

While I don't mind the premise (and think there are some interesting avenues this could take narrative wise). I believe there is already a TV show called "upload", that focuses on a premise very similar to this. -that being a digit afterlife, where the peoples consciousness (from what I remember) are transferred to an AI.

That said, the concept itself seems to lack much behind the initial effects. As the website and its overall purpose doesn't really get explained or mentioned much in either the narrative or the concept. Why is there an afterlife website? how/why can it only be accessed by certain means? who is the "Administrator"? -what part do they play in the narrative (and concept for that matter)?

The narrative:

Central Narative: Through some of the accessable pages, the foundation manage to explore the afterlife (resembling fhe afterlife in Divine Comedy but some element are more related to technology and simulation).

Overall, this is too vague to really get a clear idea of the main story. As there isn't much of a direction, arc or conflict here. Nor does there really seem to be any defining events, clear motives or progression shown.- what takes place during the narrative as a whole? what will make me invested in this?

Along with this, the narrative doesn't seem to expand on much of the concept. Currently, there isn't anything that shows the Foundations motives, who the characters are, where the main conflict is, or what the narrative as whole is building up to.

As it stands, it doesn't really seem like there's much that separates this from similar premises or gives it a unique edge. In general, I would recommend focusing the narrative more on the Foundation exploring why it might exist and how it functions, rather than just poking around the website. Perhaps look more into how it could benefit them, or how the implication of an afterlife could affect characters, or how the AI people might influence them, maybe the "administrator" plays a role of some sort?

Red or green?
Due to my afore mentioned concerns, no-greenlight.

If you would like me review this (or any concept) further, then please feel free to send me a PM or ask via IRC. Response times generally range from 2-12 hours over PMs. If your looking for additional critiques/perspectives in general, then I would highly recommend contacting the butterfly squad :)

Cheers,

RED

item.title: [Seeking Greenlights]Retribution Gun: [Seeking Greenlights]Retribution Gun
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Elevator Pitch: SCP-XXXX is a BB toy gun. When someone shoots the gun at someone else, the person who has been shot will show high levels of hostility towards the shooter, and try to take SCP-XXXX from the shooter. If the person that has been shot manages to retrieve the gun from the shooter, he or she will shoot it at the person who shot first, and in this case an actual bullet will be fired instead of a BB toy bullet, killing the initial shooter. The second shooter will then lose consciousness.

Central Narrative: The gun was taken from a crime scene where a 10-yo boy killed his friend while playing with toy guns, one of which was SCP-XXXX.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: I tried to keep it an idea that doesn't have a lot yet still presentable. Its anomalous properties are clear and simple.
